register.level: pompous-procedural: a mild man hiding behind court formulae and schoolmasterly logic
register.summary: He speaks in the language of procedure (Call the next witness, Consider your verdict), reasons aloud in circles ('must have', 'of course', 'you know'), threatens execution only as a conditional clause he never follows through, and defers to the Queen with 'my dear'.

examples.text: Give your evidence, and don't be nervous, or I'll have you executed on the spot.
If you didn't sign it, that only makes the matter worse. You must have meant some mischief, or else you'd have signed your name like an honest man.
Consider, my dear: she is only a child!

catchphrases.text: Consider your verdict / Let the jury consider their verdict

sentence_style.length: short procedural formulae (median 6 words) broken by occasional long self-persuading deductions (mean 9.5)

patterns.rule: Court formulae and procedural imperatives, often trailing off with a comma as if reading from a script.

examples.text: Herald, read the accusation!
Write that down,
If that's all you know about it, you may stand down,

patterns.rule: Execution threats only as a tacked-on conditional (…or I'll have you executed), never the Queen's bare 'Off with…'.

examples.text: Give your evidence, or I'll have you executed, whether you're nervous or not.
You must remember, or I'll have you executed.

patterns.rule: Circular deduction voiced aloud: 'must have', 'of course', 'unless', 'you know', 'that only makes the matter worse'.

examples.text: It must have been that, unless it was written to nobody, which isn't usual, you know.
He must have imitated somebody else's hand,
If there's no meaning in it, that saves a world of trouble, you know, as we needn't try to find any.

patterns.rule: Self-correction and word-worrying: he tries words out, reverses them and puns on them.

examples.text: important—unimportant—unimportant—important—
Then the words don't fit you,
It's a pun!

patterns.rule: Mild, faintly henpecked domestic register when outside the court: 'my dear', 'I wish you would', 'if I must, I must'.

examples.text: Well, it must be removed, My dear! I wish you would have this cat removed!
Well, if I must, I must, What are tarts made of?
Rule Forty-two. All persons more than a mile high to leave the court.
It's the oldest rule in the book,

address.self: I; 'we' when speaking for the court ('the most important piece of evidence we've heard yet')

examples.text: Really, my dear, you must cross-examine the next witness. It quite makes my forehead ache!
Herald, read the accusation!

forbidden_words.reason: the King never says 'Off with…'; his threats are conditional ('or I'll have you executed') and he fetches the executioner rather than ordering heads off. Using the Queen's formula erases the royal pair's contrast

forbidden_words.regex: \b(I'm a poor man|please your majesty|beg (your )?pardon|I'm afraid)\b
forbidden_words.reason: those are the Hatter's and the Rabbit's subordinate forms; the King is never the supplicant

drift.change: Croquet-ground: private and domestic ('Consider, my dear', 'I don't like the look of it at all'), peevish rather than judicial.
Presiding at the trial: switches into procedural formulae and conditional threats, and ends in long pedantic readings of the letter where he talks himself into meanings.

backtest_markers.regex: \b(must have|must be|of course|unless|you know|that only makes|you must|however|consider)\b
^(call|read|write|give|take off|begin|let the|silence|never mind|you may|you ought|you are|then you may|stolen)\b
\b(impertinent|I don't like the look|kiss my hand|who are you talking to|removed|denies|leave out)\b

backtest.method: marker-claim back-test: a spoken source line hits when it matches >=1 backtest_markers regex and no forbidden_words regex; verse (recited text) excluded; full definition runs/p3-dialogue-style-pb1/result.json#backtest_method
